Take-home Exercise 1: Geospatial Analytics for Public Good

Author

Erica Chan

Published

September 24, 2025

Modified

September 26, 2025

1. Introduction

1.1 Overview

The locations of businesses and firms are central to urban development, influencing economic growth, job creation, and the availability of resources and services for residents and other businesses. Strategic locations provide competitive advantages, access to talent and infrastructure, and impact brand image and market positioning, while also shaping the city’s overall character and functionality by fostering specialized districts and facilitating efficient supply chains and employee commutes.

In this exercise, we will apply spatial and spatio temporal point pattern analysis methods to:

Identify the “where” and “when” of new business entities, revealing clusters, patterns, and trends that are crucial for informed urban planning, resource allocation, and economic development.

Identify complex interaction patterns and emergent phenomena in the distribution of new businesses beyond simple proximity or density, such as clustering of related businesses, the influence of past trends on future locations, and the overall structural development of commercial areas, which are crucial for scientific urban planning and policy-making.

1.2 Scope

In this exercise, we will focus on various types of businesses in the F&B industry, namely restaurants, cafes, and food stalls. Our study area will cover Singapore’s core central region, which is centred around Singapore’s Central Business District and is considered the heart of Singapore’s urban area.

Our key questions are as follows: What are the spatial and temporal patterns of newly registered F&B businesses in the core central region since January 2024? Are new F&B businesses randomly distributed throughout the region and over time? If the distribution is not random, where are the areas with higher concentrations of F&B businesses?

2. Installing and Loading R Packages

The following R packages are used for this project

Package Use
sf Provides functions for importing processing and wrangling geospatial data
tidyverse Contains several core packages such as ggplot2 for data visualisation, dplyr for data manipulation, tidyr for tidying data and readr for data import from file formats like CSV
tmap provides functions for plotting cartographic quality thematic maps
httr allows interacting with web APIs and making HTTP requests. It provides a set of tools to send requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.) and process the responses received from web servers
terra Provides functions for creating, reading, manipulating, and writing raster and vector data.
spatstat To perform 1st- and 2nd-order spatial point patterns analysis and derive kernel density estimation (KDE) layer
sparr Provides functions to estimate kernel-smoothed spatial and spatio-temporal densities and relative risk functions, and perform subsequent inference
ggthemes Provides pre-built themes to ggplot2 charts
plotly Converts ggplot2 figures to interactive Plotly graphs
sparr Provides functions to estimate kernel-smoothed spatial and spatio-temporal densities
gifski Provides function to convert image files to a gif
stpp Provides functions to compute and plot spatio-temporal K function 
pacman::p_load(sf, terra, spatstat, 
               tmap, rvest, tidyverse,
               httr, ggthemes, plotly,
               sparr, gifski, stpp)

For reproducibility of results in this exercise, we will use the seed value 2025

set.seed(2025)

3. The data

To provide answers to the questions above, two data sets will be used. They are:

  1. ACRA (Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority) Information on Corporate Entities datasets from data.gov.sg, a point feature data providing both location and attribute information of registered businesses in Singapore.

  2. Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea), a polygon feature data providing information of URA 2019 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundary data.

  3. Singapore Residents by Planning Area/Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2024 (csv). This is an aspatial data file with PA and SZ fields which can be used as unique identifiers to georeference to Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary.

    • This will allow us to compare the population density with the business density of an area

3.1 Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary

3.1.1 Importing and preparing the data

The following code chunk uses the st_read function of the sf package to import the Master Plan 2019 Subzone (No Sea) dataset into R.

  • st_zm() removes Z (elevation) and M (measure) dimensions from geospatial geometries.

  • st_transform(crs=3414) transforms the projections to svy21

mpsz_sf <- st_read("data/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>%  
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
Reading layer `URA_MP19_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL' from data source 
  `C:\clyerica\ISSS626-GAA\Take-home_Ex\Take-home_Ex01\data\MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml' 
  using driver `KML'
Simple feature collection with 332 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 103.6057 ymin: 1.158699 xmax: 104.0885 ymax: 1.470775
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84

Next, the following code chunk builds the function extract_kml_field to extract REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N, SUBZONE_N, SUBZONE_C from the Description field.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {   
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") 
    return(NA_character_)         
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)   
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")      
  value <- rows %>%     
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%      html_element("td") %>%     
    html_text2()      
  
if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value 
}
mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%   
  mutate(     
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),     
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),     
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),     
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")   ) %>%   
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%   
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())

3.1.2 Filtering for study areas

For this exercise, we will focus on the planning areas within Singapore’s core central region, given its centrality and reputation as the core area for Singapore’s city life. The following code chunks filter out the central region area from the dataset and plot the area.

Note

Singapore’s Core Central Region is made up of postal districts 9, 10, 11, Downtown Core Planning Area and Sentosa. For the purposes of this exercise, we will exclude Sentosa from the study area given it is not on the main island.

cr <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(
        PLN_AREA_N == "DOWNTOWN CORE" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "MARINA EAST" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "MARINA SOUTH" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "MUSEUM" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "NEWTON" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "ORCHARD" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "OUTRAM" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "RIVER VALLEY" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "ROCHOR" | 
        PLN_AREA_N == "SINGAPORE RIVER" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "STRAITS VIEW" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "BUKIT TIMAH" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "TANGLIN" |
        PLN_AREA_N =="NOVENA" |
        PLN_AREA_N == "THOMSON"
         )

We can plot the geometry of cr to check it has been extracted as expected.

plot(st_geometry(cr))

3.1.3 Converting to owin object

spatstat relies on owin objects for observation windows to perform spatial points pattern analyses. As such, the following code chunk uses as.owin of spatstat package to convert cr from sf to owin object and checks that the class has been converted correctly.

cr_owin = as.owin(cr)
class(cr_owin)
[1] "owin"

3.2 Population data

3.2.1 Loading in the dataset

We use read_csv() to read in the Singapore Residents data as popdata

popdata <- read_csv("data/respopagesextod2024.csv")

3.2.2 Data wrangling

The following code chunk groups the population data by planning area and subzone using group_by() of dplyr package, and calculates the total population within each subzone by summing the values in the Pop column.

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`))

3.2.3 Joining attribute to geospatial data

The PA and SZ fields are converted to uppercase to allow matching with the PLN_AREA_N and SUBZONE_N fields in cr using mutate() of dpylr package.

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), 
          .funs = list(toupper))

Then, left_join() of dplyr package is used to join the population data to the geospatial data in cr.

cr <- left_join(cr, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

3.3 ACRA data

The following code chunk accesses the ACRA dataset inside the acra folder and reads it in as acra_data

folder_path <- "data\\ACRA"
file_list <- list.files(path = folder_path,
                        pattern = "^ACRA*.*\\.csv$",
                        full.names= TRUE)
acra_data <- file_list %>%
  map_dfr(read_csv,show_col_types = FALSE)

3.3.1 Tidying the data

The following code chunks perform the following:

  • selects the first 24 columns from the dataset

  • filters for the respective F&B business types of interest (Cafes, Food Stalls and Restaurants)

  • converts the string value in registration_incorporation_date to datetype and saves it under column date

  • extracts year (YEAR) and month (MONTH_ABBR) respectively from date

  • creates column MONTH_NUM which counts the number of months since Dec 2023, to create an ordinal ranking of the data by month

  • standardises the postal_code column to be 6 digits long, for later geocoding

  • Cafes
  • Foodstalls
  • Restaurants
cafes <- acra_data %>%
  select(1:24) %>%
  filter( primary_ssic_code == 56112) %>%
  mutate(date=as.Date(registration_incorporation_date),
         YEAR=year(date),
         MONTH_NUM=interval(ymd("2023-12-01"), date) %/% months(1),
         MONTH_ABBR=month(date, label=TRUE, abbr=TRUE),
         YEAR_MONTH=format(date,"%Y-%m")) %>%
  mutate(postal_code=str_pad(postal_code, width=6, side="left", pad="0")) %>%
  filter(YEAR>=2024)
foodstalls<- acra_data %>%
  select(1:24) %>%
  filter( primary_ssic_code == 56122) %>%
  mutate(date=as.Date(registration_incorporation_date),
         YEAR=year(date),
         MONTH_NUM=interval(ymd("2023-12-01"), date) %/% months(1),
         MONTH_ABBR=month(date, label=TRUE, abbr=TRUE),
         YEAR_MONTH=format(date,"%Y-%m")) %>%
  mutate(postal_code=str_pad(postal_code, width=6, side="left", pad="0")) %>%
  filter(YEAR>=2024)
restaurants <- acra_data %>%
  select(1:24) %>%
  filter( primary_ssic_code == 56111) %>%
  mutate(date=as.Date(registration_incorporation_date),
         YEAR=year(date),
         MONTH_NUM=interval(ymd("2023-12-01"), date) %/% months(1),
         MONTH_ABBR=month(date, label=TRUE, abbr=TRUE),
         YEAR_MONTH=format(date,"%Y-%m")) %>%
  mutate(postal_code=str_pad(postal_code, width=6, side="left", pad="0")) %>%
  filter(YEAR>=2024)

3.3.2 Geocoding the data

The following code chunks perform the following tasks:

  • Extracts the unique postal code for each business from the postal_code field of the tidied tibble data frame,

  • Performs geocoding by submitting the postal codes to SLA OneMap Reverse Geocode API

  • Saves the return results into two data frames namely found (for records that the postal codes are found) and not_found (for record that postal codes are not found).

  • Tidies the found data frame by only selecting the first ten columns (which contain the relevant information for our study purposes)

  • Appends the location information from found to the attribute data frame using left_join()

  • Converts the data frame to sf using st_as_sf from sf package

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
postcodes_c <- unique (cafes$postal_code)

url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"

found <- data.frame()
not_found <- data.frame(postcode = character())

for(pc in postcodes_c) {
  query <- list(
    searchVal = pc,
    returnGeom = "Y",
    getAddrDetails ="Y",
    pageNum = "1"
    )
  
res <- GET(url, query=query)
json <- content(res)

if (json$found != 0) {
  df <- as.data.frame(json$results, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  df$input_postcode <- pc
  found <- bind_rows(found, df)
  } else{
  not_found <- bind_rows(not_found, data.frame(postcode = pc))
  }
}

found <- found %>%
  select(1:10)

cafes = cafes%>%
  left_join(found,
            by=c('postal_code'='POSTAL'))

cafes_sf <- st_as_sf(cafes,
                         coords=c("X","Y"),
                         crs=3414)
postcodes_fs <- unique (foodstalls$postal_code)

url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search" 

found <- data.frame()
not_found <- data.frame(postcode = character())

for(pc in postcodes_fs) {
  query <- list(
    searchVal = pc,
    returnGeom = "Y",
    getAddrDetails ="Y",
    pageNum = "1"
    )
  
res <- GET(url, query=query)
json <- content(res)

if (json$found != 0) {
  df <- as.data.frame(json$results, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  df$input_postcode <- pc
  found <- bind_rows(found, df)
  } else{
  not_found <- bind_rows(not_found, data.frame(postcode = pc))
  }
}
found <- found %>%
  select(1:10)

foodstalls = foodstalls%>%
  left_join(found,
            by=c('postal_code'='POSTAL'))

As foodstalls includes one record with missing coordinates, we will remove this record using the following code, before converting the cleaned dataset to sf.

foodstalls_clean <- foodstalls[complete.cases(foodstalls$Y), ]

foodstalls_sf <- st_as_sf(foodstalls_clean,
                         coords=c("X","Y"),
                         crs=3414)
postcodes_r <- unique (restaurants$postal_code)

url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search"

found <- data.frame()
not_found <- data.frame(postcode = character())

for(pc in postcodes_r) {
  query <- list(
    searchVal = pc,
    returnGeom = "Y",
    getAddrDetails ="Y",
    pageNum = "1"
    )
  
res <- GET(url, query=query)
json <- content(res)

if (json$found != 0) {
  df <- as.data.frame(json$results, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  df$input_postcode <- pc
  found <- bind_rows(found, df)
  } else{
  not_found <- bind_rows(not_found, data.frame(postcode = pc))
  }
}
found <- found %>%
  select(1:10)

restaurants=restaurants%>%
  left_join(found,
            by=c('postal_code'='POSTAL'))

restaurants_sf <- st_as_sf(restaurants,
                         coords=c("X","Y"),
                         crs=3414)

3.3.3 Creating combined sf

We also create a combined sf dataframe fnb_sf with all the datapoints from all the business types studies, labelled with the business type under TYPE for later visualisation.

#add labels
restaurants_labeled <- restaurants_sf %>%
  mutate(TYPE = "Restaurants")

cafes_labeled <- cafes_sf %>%
  mutate(TYPE = "Cafes")

foodstalls_labeled <- foodstalls_sf %>%
  mutate(TYPE = "Food Stalls")

#Combine into a single sf data frame
fnb_sf <- bind_rows(restaurants_labeled, cafes_labeled, foodstalls_labeled)

As we are focusing on business in the central region, we will filter this dataset for only data points within the cr boundary using st_filter(). We plot the results to ensure it is as expected.

fnb_cr <- st_filter(fnb_sf, cr)
plot(st_geometry(cr))
plot(st_geometry(fnb_cr), add=TRUE)

4. Exploratory Data Analysis

In this section, we perform exploratory data analysis to understand underlying trends, patterns and distributions in the data.

4.1 Number of businesses registered each month

First, we will visualise the number of newly registered businesses of each type in the core central region from January 2024 to June 2025.

The following code chunk performs the following tasks:

  • uses group_by() ffrom dplyr package to group data into unique combinations of each month and business type

  • uses summarise() from dplyr to return a single row for each unique combination of the grouping variables

# Group data by business type and month, and count the number of registered businesses

fnb_by_month <- fnb_cr %>%
  group_by(TYPE, YEAR_MONTH) %>%
  summarise(num_fnb = n())

# Plot the data

ggplot(fnb_by_month, aes(YEAR_MONTH, num_fnb, color = factor(TYPE), group = TYPE)) +
geom_line() +
labs(
  title = "Number of F&B Businesses Registered by Month",
  x = "Date",
  y = "Number of Businesses",
  color = "Business type"
  ) +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Observations:

  • The number of food stalls and cafes registered in the core central region each month since January 2024 has remained relatively consistent, whereas there seems to be a downward trend in newly registered restaurants each month.

  • Restaurants are the most commonly newly registered F&B business type in the core central region; in most months, the number of newly registered restaurants is more than double the number of newly registered cafes or food stalls.

4.2 Proportion of active businesses of each type

We will also visualise the active status for each business type, derived from the entity status description. This will indicate the churn rate in Singapore’s F&B industry and if particular business types are disproportionately facing challenges causing closure.

The following code chunk allows us to examine the possible values in entity_status_description

unique(fnb_cr$entity_status_description)  
[1] "Live Company"                                 
[2] "Live"                                         
[3] "Cancelled (Non-Renewal)"                      
[4] "Struck Off"                                   
[5] "Gazetted To Be Struck Off"                    
[6] "Registration expired and has not been renewed"
[7] "Converted To LLP"                             
[8] "Ceased Registration"                          
[9] "Cancellation In Progress"

Next, the following code chunk creates column status which maps “Live Company” and “Live” values as “Active”, and maps all other values as “Not Active”. We then group the data by business type and status to find the total number of businesses of each status type. mutate() is also used to calculate the percentage of each business type of active/not active status, to be used as labels in the plotted bar graph.

# map new status values
fnb_status <- fnb_cr %>%
  mutate(status = case_when(
    entity_status_description == "Live Company" |  entity_status_description == "Live" |entity_status_description == "Converted To LLP"  ~ "Active",
    TRUE ~ "Not Active"
  ))

# Group data by business type and new status labels
fnb_by_status <- fnb_status %>% 
  group_by(TYPE, status) %>% 
  summarise(num_fnb = n())%>%
  mutate(percentage = num_fnb/sum(num_fnb)) # calculate % of active/not active for each business type for labels in graph

# Plot the graph
ggplot(fnb_by_status, aes(fill=status, y=num_fnb, x=TYPE,  label=paste0(round(percentage*100, digits = 1), "%")))+
labs(
  title = "Active Status of F&B Businesses",
  subtitle = "94.0% to 95.5% of F&B businesses in the core central region have remained active since registration.",
  x = "Business Type",
  y = "Percentage of F&B Businesses"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Active" = "darkolivegreen3", "Not Active" = "darkorange2"))+
  geom_col(position = position_stack()) +
  geom_text(position = position_stack(vjust = .5),  size=3)

Observations:

  • Restaurants seem to be slightly more successful in the core central region; while 6% of newly registered cafes and food stalls since January 2024 are no longer active, only 4.5% of newly registered restaurants are no longer active

  • However, given that restaurants have a significantly larger number of data points, this could be due cafes and food stalls having a smaller sample size.

4.3 Visualising business type density

The code chunk below performs two operations at one go for each business type. Firstly, it identifies the businesses located inside each Planning Subzone by using st_intersects(). Next, length() of Base R is used to calculate numbers of businesses that fall inside each planning subzone.

# create counts of each fnb business type
cr$cafes_count <- lengths(st_intersects(cr, cafes_sf))
cr$foodstalls_count <- lengths(st_intersects(cr, foodstalls_sf))
cr$restaurants_count <- lengths(st_intersects(cr, restaurants_sf))

#view summary statistics
summary(cr$cafes_count)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   0.000   1.000   2.507   4.000  23.000 
summary(cr$foodstalls_count)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
      0       0       1       2       3      19 
summary(cr$restaurants_count)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    0.0     0.5     3.0    10.3    13.5    84.0

Next, we create a Area column to calculate the area of each planning subzone using st_area() of sf package. This provides the area in m2. Using mutate() we then compute the density of each business type as well as the population density in each subzone in km2.

cr$Area <- cr %>%
  st_area()
cr <- cr %>%
  mutate(
    cafes_density = cafes_count/Area * 1000000,
    foodstalls_density = foodstalls_count/Area * 1000000,
    restaurants_density = restaurants_count/Area * 1000000,
    population_density = POP/Area * 1000000
    )

  geom_histogram(bins=20,

4.4 Geospatial visualisation of F&B businesses since Jan 2024

The following code chunk uses tmap to plot the distribution of the various F&B business types in the core central region, distinguished by color using fill="TYPE".

tmap_mode('view')

The above map shows most newly registered F&B businesses in core central region are located in subzones in areas such as Downtown Core, Orchard, Outram, Rochor. On the other hand, some areas such as Novena, Straits View, Marina East, and Marina South have no new F&B businesses registered.

The following code chunk sets tmap_mode back to plot.

tmap_mode('plot')

5. Spatial Point Pattern Analysis

5.1 Testing for Complete Spatial Randomness

5.1.1 Creating ppp objects

spatstat requires the point event data in ppp object form. The code chunk below uses [as.ppp()] of spatstat package to convert sf objects to ppp format. rjitter() of spatstat package applies a small random displacement to the coordinates of all the points in the ppp object, this avoids duplicate points in the object.

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
  • Combined business types
cafes_ppp <- as.ppp(cafes_sf) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
cafes_cr_ppp <- cafes_ppp[cr_owin]
foodstalls_ppp <- as.ppp(foodstalls_sf) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
foodstalls_cr_ppp <- foodstalls_ppp[cr_owin]
restaurants_ppp <- as.ppp(restaurants_sf) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
restaurants_cr_ppp <- restaurants_ppp[cr_owin]

For the combined business type ppp object, we want to ensure that the ppp object is typed using the TYPE column in fnb_sf, hence we also create a marks column in the object. factor() is used to create categorical variables from the TYPE column. We then check the final ppp object to ensure we have successfully created a multitype ppp object.

fnb_ppp <- as.ppp(fnb_sf)%>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
fnb_ppp$marks <- factor(fnb_sf$TYPE) 
fnb_cr_ppp <- fnb_ppp[cr_owin]
is.multitype(fnb_cr_ppp)
[1] TRUE

5.1.2 Rescaling ppp objects

The ppp objects are currently using meter as the unit of measurement. The following code chunk converts the unit to measurement to kilometers instead.

cafes_cr_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(cafes_cr_ppp, 1000, "km")
foodstalls_cr_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(foodstalls_cr_ppp, 1000, "km")
restaurants_cr_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(restaurants_cr_ppp, 1000, "km")
fnb_cr_ppp.km = rescale.ppp(fnb_cr_ppp, 1000, "km")

5.1.3 Performing Clark and Evans Test

Next we will perform the Clark and Evans test as a basis to test for ordering of the point event pattern of the location of newly registered businesses. We use the argument method="MonteCarlo" to compute the p-value by comparing R to the results of 999 simulated realisations of Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) with the observed number of points.

As we use argument alternative=c('two.sided') our null and alternative hypotheses are as follows:

  • H0: R=0; The point event pattern is regular or ordered

  • H1: R =/= 0; the point event pattern is not regular or ordered

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
clarkevans.test(cafes_cr_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=999)

    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 999 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  cafes_cr_ppp
R = 0.59678, p-value = 0.002
alternative hypothesis: two-sided
clarkevans.test(foodstalls_cr_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=999)

    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 999 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  foodstalls_cr_ppp
R = 0.4233, p-value = 0.002
alternative hypothesis: two-sided
clarkevans.test(restaurants_cr_ppp,
                correction="none",
                clipregion=NULL,
                alternative=c("two.sided"),
                method="MonteCarlo",
                nsim=999)

    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 999 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  restaurants_cr_ppp
R = 0.35005, p-value = 0.002
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

From the results above, as p-value<0.05 we can reject the null hypothesis at 95% confidence level and conclude that the point pattern of all newly registered F&B businesses since January 2024 are not a regular or ordered point pattern.

5.2 Visualising Kernel Density Estimation

The following code chunks compute and plots the kernel density estimation of the different F&B business types in the central region. This will allow us to compare hotspots between business types.

sigma=bw.ppl is used as based on the earlier visualisation of the geospatial distribution of F&B businesses , there are multiple areas which seem to show small clusters of F&B businesses, and other areas with empty spots. As we would like to view multiple possible clusters rather than a single tight cluster, we opt for the bw.ppl() algorithm over bw.diggle()

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
plot(density(cafes_cr_ppp.km,
             sigma=bw.ppl, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"),
     main="Cafes")
plot(density(foodstalls_cr_ppp.km, 
             sigma=bw.ppl, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"),
     main="Food Stalls")
plot(density(restaurants_cr_ppp.km, 
             sigma=bw.ppl, 
             edge=TRUE, 
             kernel="gaussian"),
     main="Restaurants")

From the heat map, the hotpots for cafes, food stalls and restaurants are all largely in the same areas (Outram, Chinatown, Downtown Core, Rochor, etc). Perhaps due to the larger sample size available, key restaurant hotspots are smaller in area, likely down to a subzone level rather than planning area.

5.3 L function

In this section, we perform Monte Carlo simulation using envelope() of spatstat package to perform a hypothesis test on whether the spatial distribution of newly registered F&B business types are clustered at different scales using the L function. The hypotheses are as follows:

  • H0: There is Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR). The points (location of newly registered cafes/food stalls/restaurants) are distributed uniformly and independently across the core central region

  • H1: The event point pattern is not a realisation of CSR.

    • If L(r) > r, the event point pattern is displaying a clustered pattern

    • If L(r) < r, the event point pattern is displaying a dispersed pattern.

Note

The code for the interactive plot of the L-function was referenced from In-Class Exercise 3a. The interactive plot allows us to zoom in and see in more detail the ranges where there is significant clustering/segregation

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
L_c.csr <- envelope(cafes_cr_ppp.km, Lest, 
                     nsim = 99, 
                     rank = 1, 
                     glocal=TRUE)
Code 
title <- "Pairwise Distance: L function"

Lcsr_df <- as.data.frame(L_c.csr)

colour=c("#0D657D","#ee770d","#D3D3D3")
csr_plot <- ggplot(Lcsr_df, aes(r, obs-r))+
  # plot observed value
  geom_line(colour=c("#4d4d4d"))+
  geom_line(aes(r,theo-r), colour="red", linetype = "dashed")+
  # plot simulation envelopes
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lo-r,ymax=hi-r),alpha=0.3, colour=c("#91bfdb")) +
  xlab("Distance r (km)") +
  ylab("L(r)-r") +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs > Lcsr_df$hi,], sides="b", colour=colour[1])  +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,], sides="b", colour=colour[2]) +
  geom_rug(data=Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,], sides="b", color=colour[3]) +
  theme_tufte()+
  ggtitle(title)

text1<-"Significant clustering"
text2<-"Significant segregation"
text3<-"Not significant clustering/segregation"

# the below conditional statement is required to ensure that the labels (text1/2/3) are assigned to the correct traces
if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs > Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){ 
  if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,])==0){ 
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){ 
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }else {
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 5) %>%

  }
} else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,])==0){
  if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%

5.4 L-cross function

Aside from the point event pattern of the individual F&B business types, we can also perform hypothesis testing to test the spatial relationship between the individual F&B business types. The hypotheses for this are as follows:

  • H0: The two point types are independent of each other

  • H1: The two point types are not independent of each other

    • If Li,j(r) is positive, this indicates there is a positive association between point types, i.e., the points are clustered around each other

    • If Li,j,(r) is negative, this indicates there is a negative association between point types, i.e., the points are dispersed or repelled from each other.

As above, we use envelope() to perform Monte Carlo simulation for this exercise.

  • Cafes & Food Stalls
  • Cafes & Restaurants
  • Food Stalls & Restaurants
L_c_fs.csr <- envelope(fnb_cr_ppp.km, Lcross, 
                       nsim=99, 
                       i="Cafes", j="Food Stalls",
                       rank=1,
                       glocal=TRUE)

      rangeslider() 
  }else {
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text2, traces = 4) %>%
      style(text = text3, traces = 5) %>%
      rangeslider() 
  }
} else if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs < Lcsr_df$lo,])==0){
  if (nrow(Lcsr_df[Lcsr_df$obs >= Lcsr_df$lo & Lcsr_df$obs <= Lcsr_df$hi,])==0){
    ggplotly(csr_plot, dynamicTicks=T) %>%
      style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%

    style(text = text1, traces = 4) %>%
    style(text = text2, traces = 5) %>%
    style(text = text3, traces = 6) %>%

  }

For all three combinations, significant clustering is consistently observed from distances as low as less than 1km. This means that not only does each F&B business type tend to cluster with other businesses of the same type, they are also likely to be located close to other types of F&B businesses.

6. Spatio-Temporal Point Pattern Analysis

In this section, we aim to analyze the spatio-temporal distribution of newly registered F&B businesses. Incorporating both spatial and temporal dimensions, will allow us to investigate how F&B hotspots evolve over time in the core central region.

6.1 Visualising geographic distribution of F&B businesses by month

Using the lapply() function from base R, we will generate individual maps displaying the point patterns of new F&B businesses as dots and save them into all_maps. The different dot colors correspond with the business type.

Then, we will create an animated gif using tmap_animation() and display the fig using the include_graphics() function from knitr package

We will create an animated GIF from the series of maps stored in the all_maps object using the tmap_animation() function from the tmap package.

Note

The code for this was modified based on the code in Christover Manafe’s Take Home Exercise 1 visualising a temporal network kernel density estimation map

all_maps <- lapply(1:max(fnb_cr$MONTH_NUM), function(i) {
  
  # filter for the month
  fnb_month <- fnb_cr %>%
    filter(MONTH_NUM==i)
  
  #create title
  title<- paste("Distribution of F&B Businesses at Month ", i)

  # Plot the map for the current month
  map <- tm_shape(cr)+
          tm_polygons() +
        tm_shape(fnb_month)+
          tm_symbols(fill="TYPE", size=0.3) +
    tm_title(title) 
  return(map)
  
})

# creating a gif with all the maps
tmap_animation(all_maps, filename = "images/fnb_animated.gif", 
               width = 1200, height = 1000, dpi = 300, delay=50)

6.2 Visualising STKDE by Month

Similarly, we will next visualise the spatio temporal kernel density estimation to view the evolution of F&B business hotspots over time. In particular, this will allow us to more easily visualise changes in hotspot intensity.

6.2.1 Extracting F&B business registration by month

The following code chunk removes unnecessary fields from the relevant sf data frames as as.ppp() only need requires mark field and geometry field.

cafes_month <- cafes_sf %>% 
  select(MONTH_NUM)
foodstalls_month <- foodstalls_sf %>% 
  select(MONTH_NUM)
restaurants_month <- restaurants_sf %>% 
  select(MONTH_NUM)

6.2.2 Creating ppp object

Next, we convert the new sf objects to ppp format as follows. We include rjitter() again to avoid issues from potential duplicate points.

cafes_month_ppp <- as.ppp(cafes_month) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
foodstalls_month_ppp <- as.ppp(foodstalls_month) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)
restaurants_month_ppp <- as.ppp(restaurants_month) %>%
  rjitter(retry=TRUE,
          nsim=1,
          drop=TRUE)

We then confirm that there are no duplicated event points using the following code chunks.

any(duplicated(cafes_month_ppp))
[1] FALSE
any(duplicated(foodstalls_month_ppp))
[1] FALSE
any(duplicated(restaurants_month_ppp))
[1] FALSE

6.2.3 Including owin object

The following code chunks combine the ppp objects with cr_owin to limit the visualisation to point events within the core central region. We then plot the owin object to check correctness of the output.

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
cafes_month_owin <- cafes_month_ppp[cr_owin]
plot(cafes_month_owin)
foodstalls_month_owin <- foodstalls_month_ppp[cr_owin]
plot(foodstalls_month_owin)
restaurants_month_owin <- restaurants_month_ppp[cr_owin]
plot(restaurants_month_owin)

6.2.4 Computing and plotting spatio-temporal KDE

Computation

The following code chunk uses BOOT.spattemp() to determine both the spatial bandwidth and the scalar temporal bandwidth for the visualisations based on bootstrap estimation. The values derives will be used as the h and lambda values when deriving the STKDE using spattemp.density.

We then plot each time slice from the resulting object and save it as a png using a for loop. The image files are then converted into a gif using gifski() from gifski package.

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
BOOT.spattemp(cafes_month_owin) 
st_kde_cafes <- spattemp.density(cafes_month_owin,
                                 h = 610,
                             lambda = 5)
summary(st_kde_cafes)

  lambda = 5 (temporal)

# find upper limit of density range to ensure fixed range for color bar when plotting
max_z <- 0
for (t_slice in st_kde_cafes$z) {
  max_z <- max(max_z, max(t_slice$v, na.rm = TRUE))
}

# iterate through each time slice and save the map as a png 

density_maps <- st_kde_cafes$z
for (i in 1:length(density_maps)) {
  # Construct a filename for each timeslice
  filename <- paste0("images/cafes/timeslice_", sprintf("%02d", i), ".png")

  # Open the PNG graphics device to start recording the plot
  png(filename = filename, 
      width = 1000, 
      height = 1000, 
      res = 100)

  # Plot the current timeslice from the list
  plot(density_maps[[i]], zlim = c(0, max_z), main = paste("Timeslice", i))

  # Close the graphics device to save the png file
  dev.off()
}

As observed earlier, the general hotspot areas remain consistent over time. However, the intensity of the hotspot has decreased since January 2024. This indicates fewer new businesses are located in these areas recently, though the area remains popular. This is not surprising given we saw earlier that the monthly count of newly registered restaurants in the central region has been decreasing. This could be due to various reasons, such as oversaturation of the market in the area, increasing barriers to entry or decreasing appeal of the area.

6.3 Spatio Temporal K function

Finally, we will use analyse whether the point patterns distribution in space and time are random or not. For this, we will use the inhomogenous K-function, which is a second order analysis, The hypotheses are as follows:

  • H0: The location and timing of event points (newly registered businesses) are independent of all other events.
  • H1: Location and timing of newly registered businesses are not independent of other new businesses.

6.3.1 Preparing spatio-temporal point process object

The following code chunk extracts the business location coordinates from the respective sf data frames.

cafes_coords <- st_coordinates(cafes_sf)
foodstalls_coords <- st_coordinates(foodstalls_sf)
restaurants_coords <- st_coordinates(restaurants_sf)

Next, we create new data frames by combining the x- and y-coordinates and temporal event (MONTH_NUM). using as.3dpoints() from stpp package then converts the data frame to spatio-temporal object class.

cafes_stpp <- data.frame(
  x = cafes_coords[, 1],  
  y = cafes_coords[, 2],
  t = cafes_sf$`MONTH_NUM`) %>%
  as.3dpoints() 
foodstalls_stpp <- data.frame(
  x = foodstalls_coords[, 1],  
  y = foodstalls_coords[, 2],
  t = foodstalls_sf$`MONTH_NUM`) %>%
  as.3dpoints() 
restaurants_stpp <- data.frame(
  x = restaurants_coords[, 1],  
  y = restaurants_coords[, 2],
  t = restaurants_sf$`MONTH_NUM`) %>%
  as.3dpoints()

The following code chunks visualises the stpp objects to check correctness of the output.

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
plot(cafes_stpp)
plot(foodstalls_stpp)
plot(restaurants_stpp)

6.3. Computing and Plotting the Spatio-Temporal K Function

Next, STIKhat() of stpp package computes the space-time inhomogenous K function. Finally, plotK() is used to visualise the output.

  • Cafes
  • Food Stalls
  • Restaurants
cafes_stik <- STIKhat(cafes_stpp)
plotK(cafes_stik)
foodstalls_stik <- STIKhat(foodstalls_stpp)
plotK(foodstalls_stik)
restaurants_stik <- STIKhat(restaurants_stpp)
plotK(restaurants_stik)

The contours show high values for relatively small values of uu and vv. This suggests that clustering occurs at short spatial and temporal distances, meaning new F&B businesses occur close to each other in both space and time for all business types.

7. Key findings and potential further research

  1. F&B businesses tend to cluster together with similar and different business types. In particular, this clustering appears most pronounced in areas such as Chinatown, Outram, Orchard, Rochor, etc. This might indicate that the industry is resilient to relatively high levels of competition within the same area. On the other hand, there are areas where there have been no new F&B business registrations over the 19 month period of study. It might be useful to study the differences in attributes of areas where there is strong clustering and where businesses are avoiding to potentially uncover key factors which encourage/discourage the F&B industry.

  2. Consistent F&B hotspots but declining intensity. While the areas mentioned above are consistent hotspots for F&B businesses, there is a decline in the number of new businesses in these areas. This may warrant further study to the reasons, whether it was due to a post-COVID-19 boom in 2024, or other reasons such as oversaturation of the market in the area, which may prompt future planning to make other areas more conducive for F&B businesses.

8. Further Improvements

This topic can be further expanded on in multiple ways to provide greater depth and strenght of analysis of the spatio-temporal patterns of newly registered F&B businesses in Singapore.

  1. Focusing on other key regions in Singapore. This exercise focused only on a section of Singapore’s central region. There are other areas which may be of interest to study, such as the Northeast region which is the most densely populated in Singapore.

  2. Focusing on different levels of areas in Singapore. This exercise used a section of a region in Singapore. It may also be of use to study spatio temporal patterns at the planning area or subzone level to see if patterns change at different spatial levels.

  3. Exploring other temporal aspects. This exercise only studied the monthly patterns of newly registered F&B businesses. It may be useful to consider other timeframes, such as quarterly or yearly. These would also allow us to use more historical data than 19 months, which may make results more robust.

  4. Incorporating other attribute/location data. It may be useful to incorporate other data which may be of interest, such as including the road networks or MRT locations to consider the accessibility factor of the businesses, or possible barriers to new businesses such as average rent prices of each area.
